title: Starting over
hookLine: Zen: start again at one. Shenxiu's verse and Huineng's on the monastery wall, and the breath count that returns to one
tomorrow: a man crossed a flood on a raft. what did he do with it after?

lines: A BIG IDEA ON THE WHITEBOARD.
WRITE A VERSE, WIN THE ROBE.
cards: Someone writes a big idea on the office whiteboard overnight, and by morning everyone's talking about it. A Zen story starts like that.
The Fifth Patriarch of Chan, the Chinese school that became Zen, tells his monks: write a verse that shows your understanding, and the one who truly sees will receive the robe.
The head monk, Shenxiu, writes his at night on a corridor wall. Then a lay worker who pounds rice out back, and can't read, hears it, and asks someone to write a second verse beside it.

teach.h: WIPE THE MIRROR AT ALL TIMES.
teach.b: Shenxiu's verse, in plain words: the body is the tree of awakening, the mind a bright mirror on its stand; wipe it with care at all times, and let no dust gather.

teach.h: FROM THE BEGINNING, NOT ONE THING.
teach.b: The rice pounder, Huineng, answered: awakening has no tree, the mirror has no stand; from the beginning there is not one thing, so where would dust gather?
The Platform Sutra says the Patriarch gave Huineng the robe, secretly, by night. But that book comes from Huineng's heirs, and Shenxiu had students of his own. So let both speak.
Shenxiu: dust really does gather. Wiping every day is honest about how a mind works. Huineng: there's nothing to get back to.
The mind was never dirty, so every moment starts whole. Here's where they meet. One common Zen practice is counting breaths, one to ten.
When you lose count, you go back to one. For Shenxiu, going back to one is the daily wiping.
For Huineng, one isn't a step backward, because nothing was lost.
Either way the Zen instruction is the same: no scolding, no catching up. Start again at one.

how: A common Zen sitting instruction is to count breaths from one to ten and return to one whenever you lose count. The verses of Shenxiu and Huineng come from the Platform Sutra.

o: going back to one, with no scolding and no catching up
throwing out your whole practice and inventing a new one
repeating a school year after failing the final exams

the Platform Sutra comes from Huineng's heirs

you go back to one, with no scolding and no catching up.

games.q: a friend in your meditation group says: my mind is a mess, so I have to wipe the mirror every single day. what's the best case for Huineng's side?
o: nothing was ever lost, so each start is whole; no need to make up for a messy day.
daily practice is pointless, so you might as well stop.
dust isn't real, so mistakes don't matter at all.
games.why: Huineng's verse says there is not one thing for dust to land on. Shenxiu says wipe every day. Both send you back to one.

practice: Close your eyes if you like, and count your out-breaths, one to ten. When you reach ten, or lose the count, go back to one, without a word to yourself about it. Keep counting until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Starting over: going back to one, as in Zen breath counting, whether you hear it as wiping the mirror or as nothing lost.

carryVoice: Your line: at one. Lose the count, begin again, no catching up. Day 1676, from one.
